- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks, especially in early/medium horizon.
- When sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates or fails to capture sharp drops; increase early-period lows and adjust downward momentum.
- Model frequently overreacts to short-term sentiment spikes (e.g., sentiment = 1.00), producing exaggerated price surges that don’t materialize — cap forecast spikes at 1.5x recent high or 20% below true outcome if sentiment is short-lived.
- Model underestimates mean reversion in medium-term (10–20 day) horizons when sentiment is neutral or mixed — add 0.1–0.3 to forecast if sentiment history shows 0.33–0.67 over 5+ days.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, model often fails to capture downward trends after sentiment shifts from positive to negative — apply a 0.5–1.0 downward bias if sentiment drops below 0.33 for 3+ consecutive days.
- If sentiment history shows alternating highs/lows (e.g., 1.00, 0.00, 1.00), model tends to overfit to recent sentiment — dampen forecast volatility by smoothing 3-day moving average of forecast values.
